The caveats ledger

Everything above should be read with these in hand. One place, linkable.

#qualification-paths · Country comparisons carry a selection effect, and it differs by major. The Open admits local and regional qualifiers and the U.S. Open runs open sectional qualifying — both dilute their host nations with club-level rounds — while a visitor who crosses an ocean to play is almost always a travelling elite. The Masters, invitational and small, has no qualifying tail at all. A country's bar mixes "how good are its players" with "how its players got in," and the mix changes depending on which majors you have switched on.
#field-gaps · Older archives thin from the bottom, and the missing names are the ones who missed the cut. Measured against each championship's own normal field size — the Masters is a small invitational by design, which is not the same thing as a gap — the emptiest first rounds here are 1983 The Open at Royal Birkdale (122 of a typical 156) · 1985 Masters at Augusta National (77 of a typical 90) · 1987 The Open at Muirfield (142 of a typical 156), and 2 championships are missing a tenth or more of their expected field. Those events therefore look slightly kinder than they were, and every early-years figure leans that way.
#venue-mix · Comparing venues is not comparing golf courses alone. A venue's rounds carry the eras it happened to host, the weather those weeks, the setup philosophy of whichever body ran the championship, and — for the one-off hosts — a single week's luck. Augusta National appears 44 times and carries a whole major's record on its own; 13 venues appear exactly once. Read a one-visit venue as one week, not as a golf course.
#no-amateur-flag · The data doesn't mark amateurs or ceremonial competitors. Their rounds are real and are counted; nothing separates a club champion qualifier from a tour professional.
#cut-truncation · Half the field has no weekend rounds. Any view touching R3–R4 describes survivors only — a better population than the one that teed off on Thursday. The cut filter makes this visible; it can't make it go away.
#par-1991 · The source data lists the 1991 Open at Birkdale as par 71; it was par 70, and every number here uses the correction. The only edit ever made to the source, and it lives in one place in the pipeline.
#small-n · Hollow marks mean the cell holds fewer than rounds — enough to plot, not enough to lean on. The footer always reports the thinnest cell in view.
